:::{#def-mgf}
#### Moment generating function

The **moment generating function** of a random variable $X$ is the function $M_X$ of a real number $t$
that gives the [expectation](expectation.qmd#def-expectation) of $\ef{tX}$,
defined at every $t$ for which that expectation is finite:

$$M_X(t) \eqdef \E{\ef{tX}}$$

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-mgf-bernoulli}
#### Moment generating function of a Bernoulli random variable

Let $X \sim \Ber(\prob)$, so $\P(X = 1) = \prob$ and $\P(X = 0) = 1 - \prob$.
For every real $t$:

$$
\ba
M_X(t)
&= \E{\ef{tX}}
&& \text{(definition of the moment generating function)} \\
&= \sum_{x \in \set{0,1}} \ef{tx} \cd \P(X = x)
&& \text{(expectation of a function of a discrete random variable)} \\
&= \ef{0} \cd (1 - \prob) + \ef{t} \cd \prob
&& \text{(substitute the Bernoulli probabilities)} \\
&= 1 - \prob + \prob\,\ef{t}
&& \text{(} \ef{0} = 1 \text{)}
\ea
$$

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#thm-mgf-moments}
#### Moments from the moment generating function

If the moment generating function $M_X(t)$ is finite for every $t$ in some open interval around $0$,
then for every positive integer $k$, the $k$-th raw moment of $X$ is the $k$-th derivative of $M_X$ at $0$:

$$\E{X^k} = M_X^{(k)}(0)$$

:::

::: proof

Let $h > 0$ be such that $M_X(t)$ is finite for every $\abs{t} < h$.
For any such $t$, the power series of the exponential gives $\ef{tX} = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \frac{t^k X^k}{k!}$.
The terms are bounded in absolute value by those of $\ef{\abs{tX}}$, a series with finite expectation,
because $\ef{\abs{tX}} \le \ef{tX} + \ef{-tX}$ and both of those have finite expectations.
So the expectation may be exchanged with the sum
(the Fubini--Tonelli theorem for sums):

$$
\ba
M_X(t)
&= \E{\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \frac{t^k X^k}{k!}}
&& \text{(power series of the exponential)} \\
&= \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \frac{t^k}{k!}\E{X^k}
&& \text{(exchange expectation and sum; linearity of expectation)}
\ea
$$

A power series is differentiable term by term inside its interval of convergence,
and the coefficient of $t^k$ in its $k$-th derivative at $0$ is $k!$ times the coefficient of $t^k$ in the series.
So $M_X^{(k)}(0) = k! \cd \frac{\E{X^k}}{k!} = \E{X^k}$.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-mgf-bernoulli-moments}
#### Moments of a Bernoulli random variable from its moment generating function

For $X \sim \Ber(\prob)$, @exm-mgf-bernoulli gives $M_X(t) = 1 - \prob + \prob\,\ef{t}$ for every real $t$,
so every derivative of $M_X$ is $M_X^{(k)}(t) = \prob\,\ef{t}$ for $k \ge 1$.
By @thm-mgf-moments, for every positive integer $k$:

$$
\ba
\E{X^k}
&= M_X^{(k)}(0)
&& \text{(moments from the moment generating function)} \\
&= \prob\,\ef{0}
&& \text{(} M_X^{(k)}(t) = \prob\,\ef{t} \text{)} \\
&= \prob
&& \text{(} \ef{0} = 1 \text{)}
\ea
$$

This agrees with the direct computation of $\E{X}$ and $\E{X^2}$ for a Bernoulli random variable
on the [expectation page](expectation.qmd#exm-lotus).

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#thm-mgf-sum}
#### Moment generating function of a sum of independent random variables

If $X$ and $Y$ are [independent](independence.qmd#def-indpt),
and $M_X(t)$ and $M_Y(t)$ are finite at a real number $t$, then:

$$M_{X+Y}(t) = M_X(t)\,M_Y(t)$$

:::

::: proof

Functions of independent random variables are independent,
so $\ef{tX}$ and $\ef{tY}$ are independent.
By @thm-indpt-uncorrelated:

$$
\ba
M_{X+Y}(t)
&= \E{\ef{t(X+Y)}}
&& \text{(definition of the moment generating function)} \\
&= \E{\ef{tX}\,\ef{tY}}
&& \text{(} \ef{a+b} = \ef{a}\,\ef{b} \text{)} \\
&= \E{\ef{tX}}\,\E{\ef{tY}}
&& \text{(expectation of a product of independent random variables)} \\
&= M_X(t)\,M_Y(t)
&& \text{(definition of the moment generating function)}
\ea
$$

:::
